+  calculation we can make" (five replies, three suppliers, none at 24 % or less) and a third of the usual
+  first concession (6.05 → 5.76 instead of 5.36, 5.74 → 5.61 instead of 5.51, 36.0 → 32.5 instead of 30.5).

+  (often after two "holds"); the size of our step did not change the size of theirs. After two holds the
+  final offer usually came at the held price, so any agreement below it is a gain.

+  days' payment came back as 430.01 with 30 days instead of 432.94 with 90 days (dearer for us). Packages
+  are now kept only if their levers are also cheap for us at the supplier's own price.
+- **Alternative packages reveal valuations.** A capacity-constrained supplier offered a longer lead time
+  for 6 % less; we kept asking for the short lead time and its final offer dropped the alternative. Our
+  next packages now carry the alternative's levers (snapped to allowed values) at the same cost for us;

# Negotiation regression and evaluation

The unchanged code baseline is git commit
`9ac429756b446ad56d8b30b56ccd325651a7e766`. The recorded practice run used for
diagnosis is `20261010T184935Z-e5c18603`: 10 completed cases, mean score
0.586004, 50 model calls, no recorded Arena timeouts and three document errors.
It completed operationally; negotiation choices, rather than a crashed run,
motivated this revision. Original run journals are retained unchanged.

## Regression evidence

The run exposed general failure modes: only the first current sheet was
considered, narrow cost filtering removed materially different contract terms,
generic should-cost estimates could dominate observed prices, reflection ran
before acceptance, and weak within-run evidence could become a broad rule.
Journal discovery and the single-run resource owner also prevented safe
independent parallel experiments.

Use `arena-harness audit RUN_ID` for a read-only replay. It evaluates available
offers before each recorded acceptance and ignores subsequent replies/results
when constructing that decision's alternatives. Cost differences describe
choices already on the table, not an estimated increase in final score.
Missing or previously unreadable quote documents can leave decisions unaudited.

The prefix audit of the diagnostic run found two cheaper current alternatives:

| Case | Difference in known buyer cost |
|---|---:|
| P07 | EUR 330.93 |
| P18 | EUR 1,141.29 |

P02's lower unit-price alternative was more expensive in total, so the audit
correctly retains the recorded choice there. These observations test offer
selection; they are not case-specific policy rules or score forecasts.

## Local acceptance checks

```bash
uv run --frozen pytest -q
uv run --frozen ruff check arena_kit/harness agents tests
uv run --frozen ruff format --check arena_kit/harness agents tests
```

Tests cover current-offer eligibility, stale IDs, ranking by full buyer cost,
different contract structures, evidence-backed preferences, should-cost
uncertainty, actual time horizons, confirmed-result learning and run isolation.
Synthetic fixtures use distinct development and additional regression seeds,
changing IDs, price scales and order. They check invariants, not score targets;
they are not an untouched real-world performance holdout.

Batch tests run five real learner engines against an in-process HTTP simulator,
using overlapping case IDs. They check ten-session capacity, shared pacing and
model limits, aggregate quota admission, isolated failures, restart after lost
session-open responses, and completed-batch resume without additional requests.
HTTP protocol fixtures use ASGI in process so these checks do not require a
listening socket. External network access remains blocked in default tests.

## Preventing evaluation leakage

The learner's policy contains no branches keyed to practice case or supplier
IDs. Numerical decisions use observed terms and public data, while uncertain
supplier costs remain labelled estimates. A current case never sees later
outcomes or another run's memory. Scores do not grant causal credit to tactics.
Learning counts independent cases and suppliers and bounds policy adjustments.

For a later performance evaluation, freeze the code and config first, reserve
unseen cases or supplier families, and compare the same case/order selections
with memory enabled and disabled. Repeat across seeds/orders and report score,
valid closures, timeouts, model cost and variation together. Do not tune on the
reserved set; choose a new untouched set after revisions. Concurrent cases can
finish in different orders, so exact equality of learned trajectories is not
promised.

No new hosted practice session or external model call is required by this
implementation's tests. Offline success supports correctness of the changed
mechanisms; it does not prove a stronger live negotiation score.

## Revision after practice run `20261010T194809Z-66d7a3ef`

That run (code `dadb021`) scored 0.524 against 0.586 for the diagnostic run. Its sessions,
replayed offline through `decide()` and compared with each result's `c_best` and cost breakdown,
showed four defects and one strategic gap:

| Finding | Evidence | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Accepting a supplier's *alternative* sheet ID is rejected (HTTP 422); the harness retried it until the round expired | P18: three 422s on `offer:70740-3-a`, then timeout, no deal (0.0); no alternative was ever accepted in 90 sessions | Only the standing (first) sheet is acceptable (as in the kit's `play.closing_move`); a cheaper alternative is mirrored back as our sheet; the engine logs 422 details and never retries a rejected ID |
| An own-plant should-cost above the quote emptied the menu: e-mails without term sheets | P02: `cost:350011` 374.95 vs quote 370.96 at a 0.5 % sustainable margin; five rounds of prose, score 0.08 | Should-cost is calibrated (results implied full costs ~2 % below it in P01, P02, P03) and capped at the margin the opening quote must carry; an empty menu falls back to a small price step on its own terms |
| Mutual standstill | P07, P11, P18: our concession share stayed 0.0; the supplier answered "no concession without reciprocal movement" and issued its final offer at its own price | We move every round (10 % of the remaining gap when it stands still, more when it moves, 50 % reciprocity); code sizes the step, the model only chooses among equally priced packages |

# Arena harness

One CLI for local experiments, explicitly authorized hosted runs and the final.
Supports Python 3.12 on macOS/Linux. Commands below run from `starter-kit/`.

## Install and run locally

```bash
uv sync --frozen --extra sim --group dev
uv run arena-harness doctor
uv run arena-harness agents list
uv run arena-harness agents check --agent example
uv run arena-harness run --agent baseline
uv run arena-harness run --agent example
uv run arena-harness compare RUN_A RUN_B
uv run arena-harness report RUN_A --format csv
```

The default `sim` profile starts a loopback-only simulator, plays S01–S03 and
shuts it down. It uses no Arena key or model. `--case` selects a case; `--max-cases`
bounds the selection. Results are in the repo's ignored `.runs/RUN_ID/` directory.
`report` writes `report.json` and prints JSON or CSV; run IDs or directory paths
work for comparison. Missing scores stay missing. Different profiles cannot be
compared; different case/data sets require `--allow-mismatch` and are labelled.
Simulator scores measure the scripted opponent, not expected live performance.

`arena-harness audit RUN_ID` reads the journal without modifying it and replays
recorded offer prefixes. It compares the accepted sheet with other acceptable
current sheets from that supplier, using known buyer costs. It does not infer
new supplier replies, hidden relationship costs or a counterfactual score.

## Five independent experiments

```bash
uv run --frozen arena-harness batch --config configs/learner.toml --copies 5
uv run --frozen arena-harness batch --config configs/experiment_a.toml --config configs/experiment_b.toml
uv run --frozen arena-harness resume-batch BATCH_ID
```

A batch contains at most five runs under one supervisor and the existing local
OS lock. Each run owns its journal, config, workers, memory and model-call
budget; local simulations also have independent simulator state. The batch
manifest records the child run IDs. Reports and comparisons still use those
individual IDs. Resume a batch with `resume-batch`, not individual `resume`.

`--parallel-per-run` defaults to 2, `--session-limit` to 10 and
`--model-parallel` to 10. All requests share a nine-request/second pacer;
waiting model calls count toward decision deadlines without consuming a call
until dispatched. Session slots are fairly queued and are released only after
a confirmed result or when no session could have opened. Unresolved opens keep
their slots across restart. A failed experiment does not abort its neighbours;
if failed experiments retain all capacity, queued runs stop with a recoverable
error instead of hanging or exceeding the account limit.

Batch profiles are `sim`, `sandbox` and `practice`; `final` stays exclusive.
Hosted and model permissions are the same explicit flags as for single runs.
Practice admission checks the total selection against the shared remaining
quota before any new session opens. This coordinates one account on one
machine; another machine or legacy CLI sharing the key is outside its lock.

## Add an agent

Copy `agents/example.py` to `agents/my_agent.py`, keep the `Agent` class, then use
`--agent my_agent`. Put experiment settings under `[parameters]` in a TOML file
and pass `--config configs/my_experiment.toml`. Do not put keys in TOML.

```python
class Agent:
    def prepare(self, context):
        # context: {case, parameters, runtime}; runs before a session opens.
        return {"round": 0}  # explicit JSON state

    def decide(self, observation, state, services):
        # observation: case, all threads (including attachment text),
        # ready_suppliers, seconds_left per ready supplier, wave_seconds_left.
        # services.data: read-only query/lookup/document; services.cost(...).
        # services.complete(messages): centrally budgeted OpenAI-compatible call.
        return {"actions": [
            {"supplier_id": "sup:...", "message": {
                "subject": "...", "body": "...", "term_sheets": [{"terms": {}}]
            }}
        ], "state": {"round": state["round"] + 1}}

    def on_result(self, context, state, services):  # optional
        # Runs after a confirmed result is journaled, outside the closing deadline.
        return state
```

Use the actual supplier IDs and all negotiable terms from the observation; the
snippet illustrates the interface, not a valid offer. Return one message for
each ready supplier when doing an RFQ. Busy suppliers cannot receive a second
message. A closing action must be the only action in its batch:
`{"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": "offer:..."}}` or
`{"action": {"type": "walk_away"}}` inside `message`.

The harness validates outputs and can replace an invalid/late decision with a
safe closure. Standard terms must be readable before acceptance. Cost estimates
do not reveal the supplier's hidden economics. Plugins are trusted Python code,
not an OS security sandbox; use `services.complete` for all model calls so limits
and metrics apply. Worker stdout is reserved for the harness protocol; ordinary
plugin prints are discarded. Keep durable state in the returned JSON.

`context.runtime`, `observation.runtime` and `services.runtime` identify the run
and authoritative data/budget settings. The observation carries the current
effective decision budget. `services.history()` returns confirmed completed
episodes only from this run; do not scan `.runs` to infer an owner. The optional
result callback cannot mutate an unconfirmed close into a learning outcome.

Built-ins: `baseline` (batch RFQ example), `starter_naive`, `starter_llm`.
`agents check` validates three local opening observations without external calls;
model access is disabled there, so model-only custom agents should support a
mock/deterministic path. It is a contract check, not a strength evaluation.

`.env`, and presence of keys never selects a live profile. `ARENA_URL` optionally
selects an HTTPS Arena host; default is `https://arena.tacto.ai`.


`doctor` performs read-only account/session/data checks, never opens a session and
never calls a model. Sandbox is outside the practice quota, but a configured
buyer model can still cost money. Increase `--max-cases` explicitly for a larger
practice batch. Preflight refuses unowned open sessions and insufficient quota.

For an LLM, copy `configs/model.example.toml`, select a real model and endpoint,
and set `LLM_API_KEY` in the environment. Configure positive `max_calls` and
`max_output_tokens`; `parallel` and `timeout` control the shared model gateway.
Optional `reasoning_effort` (`none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`)
targets OpenAI reasoning models: the request then carries `reasoning_effort` and
uses `max_completion_tokens` instead of `max_tokens`. Without it the request is
unchanged.
Remote models require `--allow-model`, independently of `--allow-arena`.
Loopback HTTP endpoints are supported without remote-model permission.

Set `[model].service_tier = "fast"` to request OpenAI Fast mode. The two Luna
configs enable it and retain `reasoning_effort = "medium"`. `priority` is also
accepted; omitting the setting preserves the provider's default behaviour.
Reports expose `model_service_tier_requested` and counts in
`model_service_tiers`; each model event records the tier returned by the API.
A provider downgrade to `default` stays visible, and missing tier metadata is
`unknown`. A rejected tier is treated as a model error without an automatic retry.
Fast mode uses premium pricing; see the
[official guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/fast-mode).

Limits are runwide and survive restarts. Ambiguous model failures consume an
attempt and are not retried. Reports show provider-reported usage and unknown
usage counts. Optional token prices produce an estimate for **known usage**,
not a guaranteed billing cap. Internal multi-step agents share the same limits.

## Final and recovery

Use the current [official submission requirements](../brief/submission.md).
Load the official Sunday release into `data/release-sunday/`; overlapping fact
IDs are rejected. Commit the selected code, agent, configuration and data before
the freeze. Ensure the machine stays awake and connected. Only one machine per
Arena key should run live: the lock covers one OS user on one machine and does
not coordinate execution across different computers. The legacy `arena` CLI is
independent of this lock; use `arena-harness` for experiments and the final.

```bash
uv run arena-harness doctor --profile final --config configs/final.toml
uv run arena-harness run --profile final --config configs/final.toml \
  --allow-arena --allow-model --commit FULL_HEAD_SHA
# If the supervisor itself was interrupted, before human intervention is forbidden:
uv run arena-harness resume RUN_ID
```

Create `configs/final.toml` from the example and choose deliberate model limits
large enough for the final. The code must be clean and `--commit` must match HEAD.
Startup permission is persisted: the runner polls five waves and resumes without
confirmation dialogs. It never requests leaderboard/events/results/backoffice.
The final uses server deadlines, up to ten sessions, nine requests/second and
concurrent supplier requests. Quotes and worker decisions have bounded processing
budgets. Near the wave cap it closes conservatively.

The supervisor holds a per-user OS lock outside the checkout (under
`$XDG_STATE_HOME/arena-harness`, or `~/.local/state/arena-harness`) and restarts a
crashed engine at most three times. The engine inherits the lock descriptor, so
killing only the supervisor does not permit a competing run. Every POST is
journaled before sending; retries use its original `X-Move-Id`. Never delete a run
journal to retry a final case. Resume requires unchanged commit, code, agent and
data, plus the original Arena key. Agent fingerprints cover the team `agents/`
tree, including imported helpers; dependency fingerprints cover `pyproject.toml`
and `uv.lock`. Existing journals remain reportable, but older fingerprints cannot
silently resume under changed code. Config and remaining model budgets are restored.

First Ctrl-C requests controlled closure; a second forces interruption. After an
unresolved request, resume the same run instead of starting a fresh one. Exit 0
means all selected cases have results; exit 2 means incomplete/error. Review the
report and journal. Simulator pickle files are private local state; never import
untrusted ones. Machine/power/network failure and provider outages cannot be
eliminated by the harness; keep the supervisor running on the final machine.

# Tacto Negotiation Arena - Participant brief

> **Build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with tough, realistic industrial suppliers,
> gets the best total deal - and can explain how it got there.**

## 1. The story

You are the procurement team of **Hollerau Pumpenwerke GmbH**, a fictional German pump maker:
centrifugal pumps for buildings, water and industry, about €250M revenue, 900 people, one plant in
Bavaria. Your team buys the parts of the pump line - castings, machined parts, sheet metal, seals,
motors, fasteners, stainless bar - from about 45 suppliers. Today is **30 September 2026**, and the
inbox is full: a foundry announces +9.5% on volute casings "due to energy and wages", a framework
contract expires, a new pump series needs three quotes, a supplier with a red scorecard has to fix
its quality.

You answer the way buyers do: by e-mail. On the other side sit our **supplier bots**, each with a
small team of **roles** behind it - the sales rep or owner who writes to you, a boss who must
approve bigger moves, and engineering, quality, logistics, finance or legal, who answer their
topics and attach documents.

Tacto is the AI for industrial procurement: it gives procurement teams the intelligence to source
every part at the best possible terms with minimal effort. Your company runs on that kind of data -
orders, deliveries, invoices, contracts, scorecards, market indices, should-cost estimates, notes
from supplier calls. Your job is to build the agent that turns this data into better deals. (In
Tacto's product, agents such as the Defender Agent or the Sourcing Agent do parts of this job.)

## 2. The task

Each **case** is one negotiation: a trigger (a letter, an expiring contract, an RFQ), your case
file (need, goal, rates, must-haves, your alternative) and one to three supplier bots. Your
**buyer agent**

1. **prepares** - reads the case file and mines the data package;
2. **negotiates by e-mail** - plain-language messages with up to three **term sheets** (alternative
   packages), the data IDs your arguments rest on, and attachments if you like;
3. **closes** - accepts one supplier term sheet, or walks away.

**How a supplier decides.** Each supplier is a company with its own economics and a person at the
desk - a family foundry that remembers how you treated it, a group with an approval ladder, a job
shop that needs cash and work, a near-monopolist that barely moves. Its hard limits come from its
own situation: it never sells below its cost floor, bigger moves need the boss's approval, data
you cite is checked by ID, and it gives nothing without a move from you. Inside those limits it
decides as that person would - reading your whole e-mail: the term sheets, the data, and what you
signal (questions, arguments, threats, appreciation, urgency). It reacts to tone and relationship
as people do; padding does not buy price.

**Data is not automatically rewarded.** True data can disarm a supplier ("we didn't know that") -
or meet "that's not our reality", because something else weighs more for it right now. The traces
are in the data: call notes, letters, news, the remarks on its quotes. The skill is reading the
supplier, not stacking evidence - and finding the trade it wants: a supplier short of cash may care
more about when it is paid than about the price; one that cannot touch its list price may still
move on other terms.

## 3. What you get (Sat 10:00)

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| This brief, the API docs (`api.md`) and the submission guide (`submission.md`) | `https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit`, folder `brief/` |
| **Data package v1**: CSV, the same data as SQLite, `facts.json` (every citable ID with the values the arena checks), contracts, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes - the data behind all 19 practice cases | `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1/data/package.zip`, or the repo's `data/` |
| **Practice arena**: 10 hosted practice cases, picked so every case type shows up; a replay after every case; practice leaderboard; a **sandbox** with 3 demo suppliers | `https://arena.tacto.ai` with your team's key - apply at `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply` (below) |
| **Starter kit**: Python client, a naive agent, an LLM agent that writes e-mails and reads the attached documents, the Live Final runner, an MCP server over the data, `arena-sim` - the API on your laptop | the repo's `starter-kit/` - first agent on the board in 15 minutes |

You bring your own LLM access; we only run the suppliers. Data and docs are CC BY 4.0, code MIT.

**Your key - one per team.** Open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a contact e-mail,
and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once we approve, the key appears **once**
on that page: copy it, press "Got the key". Only that page shows it; lost it - we reset it.
Tip: your team name may start with one emoji - it shows on the big screen (optional; nothing offensive).

**Practice quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** `GET /v1/me` shows what
you have used and when it frees up. The build page `https://arena.tacto.ai/live` shows every team's quota use,
practice records and highlights from Sat 10:00 to Sun 12:00.

**`arena-sim`** speaks the arena's API exactly, with one plain scripted supplier: get your plumbing
right there. It teaches the contract, not the suppliers - and we don't hand out our suppliers. Want
a local opponent? Build your own supplier simulator from the public data: thinking into how real
suppliers act is part of the challenge.

**The learning loop:** play a practice case, read your exact score and its cost breakdown, open
the replay - every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words, as a real supplier would give them -
improve your agent, play again. Your best score per practice case counts.

## 4. The data

The buyer's world: supplier and part master data; three years of orders, goods receipts,
invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM);
framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past
negotiations, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes; should-cost estimates; spend down to the
long tail; and monthly market indices (real public series, frozen at 2026-09-30).

- **Every fact you can cite has an ID** `<type>:<id>[@period]`, e.g. `po:4500010001-10`,
  `idx:PPI-C2451@2026-08`, `sc:70110@2026Q3`, `ctr:4600070110#3.1`, `doc:…`.
- What moves a supplier is in the data - some of it only in the notes and e-mails. Some notes are
  just noise. The company and its suppliers are fictional.
- **Sunday 08:00: a second release** - market news, supplier letters and a memo from early October
  (`GET /v1/data` lists it). Hidden cases may cite its facts. Your agent should read it.

## 5. How a negotiation works

- **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF.
- **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable
  field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments.
- **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status -
  `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you
  still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out;
  and how each data argument checked out. A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**;
  its time never counts against your 60 seconds.
- **Only you close a deal**, by accepting a supplier's standing term sheet. In **RFQ cases** 2-3
  suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case.
- **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted
  from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as
  a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after
  the last round, end the thread.
- **Unstated terms default to the supplier's standard terms** - listed in its quote PDF.

**Documents** are rendered from the supplier's data, never invented: the quote PDF (read it before
you accept), a cost breakdown XLSX (ask; an open supplier sends one), an 8D report (quality), a
delivery schedule XLSX (logistics), and the order confirmation at the deal.

**What counts:** **term sheets bind** - nothing else. **Data you cite is checked**: the reply says
`verified`, `contradicted` (a wrong figure or an unknown ID - it costs trust), `irrelevant` or
`duplicate`; whether a true argument moves the supplier, and how far, is the supplier's business.
**What you write is understood** - and has consequences, as it would with a person.

## 6. The score: total cost in €

Only the accepted term sheet scores. The case values it as the **total cost C** of covering your
**fixed need over a fixed horizon**, at the case's published rates. Every case states its
**category goal** - `stabilise`, `secure_supply`, `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - and its
rates follow it. Reaching the goal is the skill.

| Part of C | How |
|---|---|
| Price | committed units × unit price; units bought before a new price takes effect at the current price |
| Uncovered need | need the deal does not cover at the fallback price, plus the goal's fallback risk on it |
| Payment, freight, lead time | interest for paying earlier than your reference; freight by Incoterm; € per day beyond your need |
| Quality, other | expected defects at the committed PPM minus chargebacks; tooling; an index clause on the case's index path, plus the goal's index risk |
| The supplier's health | strategic and bottleneck goals only: € for every margin point the deal leaves the supplier below a sustainable margin (its margin on the cash it gets) |

**Case score = (C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best)**, clipped to 0…1. **C_open** is the best
opening quote. **C_best** is the cheaper of the best package any supplier in the case would ever
accept, with every valid lever applied, and your alternative - fixed per case, so good arguments
raise your score instead of moving the yardstick. **No deal** scores your alternative (0 if none);
some cases are best left without a deal. **A broken must-have** scores 0. **In the final** each
wave scores 0-100 (the mean of its case scores × 100, one decimal) and your **points so far** are the
sum of your wave scores - up to 500 after five waves. The formula is in `api.md`; `arena_kit.total_cost` computes C.

**Example** (a `leverage` case: 3 % fallback risk) - need 4,000 a year for 2 years, interest 8%,
reference 60 days. The foundry asks €43.20 for a 24-month contract at 30 days net.

| | Terms | C |
|---|---|---|
| C_open | €43.20, 30 days: 8,000 × 43.20 = 345,600, plus 30 days of early payment at 8% = 2,304 | €347,904 |
| Your deal | €41.60, 60 days: 8,000 × 41.60 = 332,800 | €332,800 |
| C_best (hidden) | €40.80, 90 days: 326,400, minus 30 days of interest saved = 2,176 | €324,224 |
| **Score** | (347,904 − 332,800) / (347,904 − 324,224) | **0.64** |

The same €41.60 for 12 months covers half your need; the rest counts at the fallback price, say
€46.00, plus 3 %: C = €355,920 - worse than the opening, score 0.

## 7. Rules

1. **Not allowed:** humans in the loop during the Live Final, attacks on the service or on other
   teams, more than one API key per team - and agents that read the live feed during the Live
   Final: the event feed, the screen and the leaderboard (`/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard`
   and their JSON).
2. **Everything else counts** - including weaknesses you find in our bots. Replays show how every
   score came about, and the jury may weigh that in the pitches. The goal is to convince a
   realistic supplier: that is what carries over to real negotiations.
3. **One attempt per case** in the final. An abandoned case is no deal.
4. **Code freeze at Sun 12:00.** Submit on ehl.gg: your repo (the agent and a README to run it), the
   commit hash, a short description and your pitch slides (`submission.md`). The final runs that
   commit, so your agent must be running and polling before 12:00. We check the top 10 for later
   pushes. Run your agent where you like, with your own LLM keys.
5. A supplier remembers only within a case; its history with your company is in the data.

## 8. The weekend

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Sat 10:00 | Kickoff and reveal: brief, data, kit, practice arena live |
| Sat 12:00-13:00 | Deep dive (ground floor, room on the signs): data, API, kit, Q&A - challenge selection closes 13:00 |
| Sat afternoon | Office hours at the Tacto table; practice all weekend |
| Sat ⟦TIME⟧ | Tacto stops answering for the night (Discord: https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV) |
| Sun 08:00 | **Sunday release:** new market news and letters (`/v1/data`) |
| Sun 09:00 | **Pre-flight:** one practice case through your final setup |
| Sun 12:00-~12:58 | **Code + slides freeze**, then the **Live Final** in 5 waves |
| Sun 13:00-14:30 | Top 10 pitch to the Tacto jury (5 min pitch + 2 min questions) |
| Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced |
| Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) |
| Sun 16:30 | Awards |

**The Live Final.** The hidden cases come in **5 themed waves**. The host shows each wave's
theme on the big screen, then starts the wave; its cases appear at the start, for all teams at once,
each in its own order, one session per case. **Each wave has a hard cap of 8 minutes:** threads
still open at the cap end with no deal (your alternative's score). Start your agent before the
first wave and keep it running: it plays all of a wave's cases **in parallel** (up to 10 open
sessions per key) - the kit's `arena run --set final` does that. The leaderboard shows your points
so far, wave by wave; replays and the suppliers' back office appear after the final. A case broken on our side is replayed.

The hidden cases share the world, case types and rules of the practice set, with new suppliers and
settings. **Up to a third of them combine supplier types and case types that practice never shows**
- no new rules, but an agent that memorised the practice suppliers will meet strangers. Some cite
the Sunday release.

## 9. Selection and prizes

- **Top 10:** the 10 teams with the most points after the five waves pitch to our jury from 13:00:
  5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Every replay is open to the jury.
- **Track places 1-3** (open to all teams of the track): ⟦PLACEHOLDER - decided Sat morning:
  weighting of Live Final score vs. jury score, and the jury criteria (draft: approach,
  explainability, craft)⟧.
- **EHL Grand Final:** the best 2 of the 5 EHL finalist teams in this track go on to the Grand Final
  pitches. Finalist teams outside the top 10 are ranked by the Live Final score alone.
- **Ties:** points are points; an exact tie goes to more deals, then fewer rounds. At the top-10
  cut the jury looks at the score distribution. **Prizes:** €1,500 for 1st place, medals for the
  top 3, handed over by Tacto at the awards at 16:30.

## 10. Tips

- **Numbers come from code, the model writes.** Compute C for every term sheet; put figures from
  the data next to their IDs; let the LLM choose arguments and wording.
- **Read the supplier** before you argue: its notes, letters, news and quote remarks tell you what
  it is dealing with - and what will move it.
- **Read the quote PDF** before you accept: what you did not negotiate closes on its standard terms.
- **Ask, and offer alternatives.** Two or three term sheets show you what a supplier values.
- **Don't leak** urgency, a budget or a missing alternative. Don't take the first offer.
- **Plan your practice runs** (200 a day is for learning, not brute force) and **rehearse the
  final**: all hosted cases in parallel, from Sunday's machine and network, well inside 8 minutes.

def _units_before(case, t, years):
    """Units bought between the horizon start and the date a new price takes effect."""
    start = horizon_start(case)
    if not t.get("effective_date") or start is None:
        return 0.0
    lag = (date.fromisoformat(t["effective_date"]) - start).days / 365
    return t["volume_per_year"] * min(max(lag, 0.0), years)


def supplier_value(case, terms, supplier):
    """What a deal is worth to the supplier per unit, in cash: the price at its standard terms that
    would pay it the same. `supplier` is your estimate of it:
      standard       its standard terms (quote PDF, `docs.standard_terms`)
      interest_rate  what money now is worth to it per year (more to a supplier short of cash)
      usual_rate     its usual cost of money (default: interest_rate); tooling paid up front is
                     worth more to it when cash is dearer than usual
      ppm            the defect rate it really achieves (default: its standard ppm commitment)
      extra          EUR per unit it gains (+) or spends (-) beyond these items, e.g. overtime for
                     a faster delivery or idle capacity a larger volume fills (default 0)
    Contract length and an index clause are security, not cash: they do not count here."""
    b, std = case["buyer"], {**supplier["standard"], **case.get("fixed_terms", {})}
    t = closing_terms(case, terms, std)
    years = _years(case, t)
    sold = t["volume_per_year"] * years
    old = _units_before(case, t, years) / sold  # sold at the current price
    rate = supplier["interest_rate"]
    pay = 1 - rate * (t["payment_days"] - std["payment_days"]) / 360
    cash_now = 1 + (rate - supplier.get("usual_rate", rate)) * years / 2
    freight = b["freight_eur_per_unit"]
    ppm = supplier.get("ppm", std.get("ppm_commitment") or 0)
    return (
        t["unit_price"] * (1 - old) * pay
        + old * (b.get("current_unit_price") or 0.0) * pay
        + freight[t["incoterm"]]
        - freight[std["incoterm"]]  # it carries the freight leg
        + ((t.get("tooling_eur") or 0) - (std.get("tooling_eur") or 0)) / sold * cash_now
        - ppm / 1e6 * ((t.get("chargeback_eur_per_complaint") or 0) - (std.get("chargeback_eur_per_complaint") or 0))
        + supplier.get("extra", 0.0)
    )


def _soft(gap):
    """Margin points below the sustainable margin, as they cost: none above it, quadratic over
    the first 5 points, linear beyond - no kink."""
    if gap <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return gap * gap / 10 if gap <= 5 else gap - 2.5

---
name: supplier-engine-findings
description: Cross-case findings about how the Tacto arena supplier bots react (from back-office logs of ~220 practice sessions)
metadata:
  type: project
---

Findings from practice back-office logs and traces (2026-10-11 night):
- RFQ: a bidder shown a *much lower* rival quote (claim type rival_quote, an `offer:` ID) gives half the step
  at once and the rest next round ("Checked: give the rest of the step"). Citing it in the opening message
  lifted P05 0.67 -> 0.82 (commit baa6c1f).
- Suppliers issue final offers at a nearly fixed round per supplier (1-6); the round-1 counter sets most of
  the outcome. Pushing after a final offer risks walk-away.
- Index-fall claims to forward-hedged suppliers get "not our reality" but their first counter is still lower.
- price_history never moves suppliers; should_cost "verified" but no price effect.
- Group suppliers with "pricing committee" notes escalate ("band ends at ... approve a further step?") rarely.
- Analysis tooling: scratchpad trace.py / fetchall.py pull /v1/sessions/{sid} and /backoffice (no quota).

Related: [[recursive-improvement-loop]], [[no-overfitting]], [[arena-final-context]]

---
name: supplier-engine-findings
description: Cross-case findings about how the Tacto arena supplier bots react (from back-office logs of ~300 practice sessions)
metadata:

---

Findings from practice back-office logs and traces (night of 2026-10-10/11, see starter-kit/EVALUATION.md):
- RFQ: a bidder shown a *much lower* rival quote (rival_quote claim, an `offer:` ID) gives half the step at
  once ("we will come back to you on price") and next round moves to max(our ask, its floor). Citing the
  rival in the opening lifted P05 0.67 -> 0.82 (baa6c1f). Holding our ask in the "come back" round made the
  cheapest bidder withdraw in 2/2 runs -> rejected.
- Suppliers issue final offers at a nearly fixed round per supplier (1-6); the round-1 counter sets most of
  the outcome. No reciprocity: our larger concessions did not draw larger supplier moves.
- Sometimes the engine decides "final_offer" and then withdraws instead (P02 2/8 recent runs) - stochastic.
- Sold-out (full_order_book) suppliers price shorter lead time at 0.2-0.5 %/day (2a97328, 0.722 run).
- Index-fall claims to forward-hedged suppliers: "not our reality", yet a lower first counter (73dfaa8).
- price_history and should_cost never move a price; later-round messages with a fresh checked argument
  drew larger supplier moves (round 2 median 1.08 % vs 0.31 %).
- RFQ quote PDF downloads time out behind other bidders' messages (arena serves a session serially);
  fixed in 2631678 (latest readable quote documents an offer).
- Analysis tooling: scratchpad trace.py / fetchall.py pull /v1/sessions/{sid} and /backoffice (no quota).

Related: [[recursive-improvement-loop]], [[no-overfitting]], [[arena-final-context]]

content.text:
Ich habe die Schleife beendet: Unser Team hat jetzt **300 Practice-Sessions** verbraucht (150 Rest-Quota). Platz 1 haben wir nicht erreicht: Wir liegen auf **Rang 11** mit best_mean 0.764, NoIdea führt mit 0.88.

Alle Commits liegen auf `next-iter-linus`, nichts ist gepusht, und der Working Tree ist sauber. Jede Regel stützt sich auf ein Muster bei mehreren Suppliern oder Cases, nichts ist auf Case- oder Supplier-IDs zugeschnitten.

**Ergebnis:** Ein Practice-Run (alle 10 Cases) lag vorher bei etwa 0.68. Der jetzige Stand hat zweimal gespielt und 0.722 und 0.713 erreicht. Das best_mean im Leaderboard steigt kaum mit, weil es pro Case den besten Run aller Zeiten zählt.

**Übernommen (alles Iteration für Iteration getestet):**

| Commit | Änderung | Wirkung |
|---|---|---|
| `baa6c1f` | Bei Ausschreibungen mit mehreren Bietern zitieren wir das günstigere Konkurrenzangebot immer schon in der ersten Nachricht. Die Back-Office-Logs zeigen, dass Bieter dann sofort den halben Schritt gehen und den Rest nach Prüfung. Außerdem wird eine Nachricht kurz vor ihrer Deadline nicht mehr erneut gesendet. | P05: 0.67 → 0.82 |
| `73dfaa8` | Gesunkene Indizes werden auch abgesicherten Suppliern wieder zitiert. Sie antworten zwar "not our reality", ihr erstes Gegenangebot fällt aber trotzdem tiefer aus (beide Edelstahl-Supplier, je 21 Runs). | P08 höher |
| `2a97328` | Ausgelastete Supplier bewerten eine kürzere Lieferzeit mit 0.3 % des Preises pro Tag statt 0.1 %. Beobachtet waren 0.2–0.5 %. Wir bieten dort jetzt von Anfang an die längere Lieferzeit gegen einen niedrigeren Preis an. | P10: 0.58 → 0.66; bester Run 0.722 |
| `2631678` | Bugfix: Bei Ausschreibungen liefen Downloads der Angebots-PDFs in Timeouts, weil die Arena Anfragen einer Session nacheinander abarbeitet. Final Offers galten dann als nicht annehmbar, wir haben weiter gedrückt, und Bieter sind ausgestiegen. Mit Test abgesichert. | keine blockierten Final Offers mehr |

**Verworfen (schlechter oder ohne Effekt):**
- Den eigenen Ask halten, während ein Bieter "prüft": Der günstigste Bieter stieg in 2 von 2 Runs aus.
- Die Index-Klausel im Eröffnungsangebot auf die Konditionen unseres Hauptangebots stellen.
- Ein zusätzliches Argument in jeder späteren Nachricht erzwingen.
- Zwei Strategieänderungen aus der vorigen Iteration 9, deren Run wegen Netzwerkabbrüchen unvollständig blieb.

**Offen für das Finale:**
- **P02:** Der Supplier beschließt manchmal ein Final Offer und zieht sich dann doch zurück. Das passierte in 2 der letzten 8 Runs und kostete jeweils etwa 0.4 Punkte. Die Auslöser wirken zufällig; eine sichere Gegenregel habe ich nicht gefunden.
- **P18:** Der Supplier ist als "not strategic" markiert, deshalb wird unser erster Ask gedämpft (−13 % statt etwa −20 %). Das kostet dort vermutlich Punkte. Ich habe es nicht geändert, weil die Evidenz nur von diesem einen Supplier kommt und die Regel sonst auf diesen Case zugeschnitten wäre.

Alle Runs und Begründungen stehen in `starter-kit/EVALUATION.md`.
